name: The Cape With Its Eave Raised

severity_by_style.why: The eave height is the type's defining measurement; raised, the type is gone whatever the trim does.
As above, and this is where it actually happens.
A full two-storey colonial has no eave-height rule of this kind; the fault only bites where a Cape is being claimed.
The type is story-and-a-half by economy rather than by rule.

symptom: A Cape Cod with its eave 11 to 13 ft above the first floor instead of 8 ft to 9 ft 6 in, and a band of blank siding between the first-floor window heads and the cornice. The pitch may still be 10:12 and the trim may be immaculate, but the house has become a small two-storey colonial wearing a Cape's roof. The elevation is now half wall and half roof, where a Cape is one third wall and two thirds roof.

cause.explanation: IRC R305.1 requires 7 ft 0 in of ceiling height in habitable space, and R305.1.1 requires that height over at least 50 per cent of the required floor area in a sloped-ceiling room. Under a 10:12 roof on a 28 ft deep house, the area meeting that test is small, and every inch the plate rises converts unsaleable roof volume into countable, appraisable floor. Raising the plate 16-24 in typically adds 300-400 sf of habitable second floor. It is the single most profitable twenty inches on a small plan, and it is decided in a framing conversation, not a design one.
cause.cost_saved: Roughly $2,500-5,000 of extra framing and siding to gain 300-400 sf, which is $8-15 per sf against a build cost several times that. Nothing else on the house has that return.

rule_violated.statement: Eave height 8 ft 0 in to 9 ft 6 in above finished first floor, and the head of the first-floor window not more than 14 in below the underside of the cornice. This single rule separates every real Cape from every revival Cape.
Wall to roof height ratio on the front elevation about 1:2 - the entire house reads as roof.

7 ft 0 in ceiling height in habitable space, over at least 50 per cent of the required floor area where the ceiling is sloped. Under a 10:12 roof on a 28 ft depth the compliant area is small, and every inch the plate rises converts unsaleable roof volume into countable floor.

correct_practice: The Cape's defining rule is the eave DOWN. Eave 8 ft 0 in to 9 ft 6 in above finished first floor; the head of the first-floor window within 14 in of the underside of the cornice, with no frieze between them; ground-floor ceiling 6 ft 10 in to 7 ft 6 in; ridge 18-22 ft above grade; roof 9:12 to 12:12; depth 26-30 ft. The upstairs comes out of the roof volume and is paid for with pitch and depth, not with wall. Where a full second storey is genuinely required, the honest answers are other types that exist for the purpose: a garrison, a New England two-storey colonial, or a story-and-a-half with rear shed dormers.

fixes.right: Drop the plate back to 8 ft 6 in - 9 ft 0 in and take the second-floor area in depth (28-30 ft) and pitch (11:12 or 12:12) instead of in wall height.
fixes.cheap: Keep the raised plate at the back and drop the front eave to Cape height, taking the headroom in a rear shed dormer running 50-75 per cent of the roof length and set back 18-36 in from the rear wall plane. The street elevation is restored at effectively zero cost, and rear-slope dormers on a Cape are a permissible later addition in the type's own terms.
fixes.dishonest: Holding the eave high and shrinking the first-floor windows so the 14 in head-to-cornice relationship is satisfied at a smaller scale. This produces a Cape with mean little windows, which is a worse building than an honest two-storey.

test.note: The single most reliable Cape measurement, and it needs no scale reference because it is a ratio between two things in the same photograph. A real Cape reads under 0.25; a raised-eave revival reads 0.5-0.9. The absolute rule behind it is that the window head sits within 14 in of the underside of the cornice with no frieze between them.

secondary_tests.note: A Cape is about 1:3 - the entire house reads as roof, with the wall roughly one third of the elevation and the roof two thirds. The fault reads 0.5 or greater.
8 ft 0 in to 9 ft 6 in. This is the constraint the whole type hangs on, and it is the one the framer changes.
9:12 to 12:12. The upstairs is paid for with pitch and depth, not with wall.

detection: In a straight-on photograph of the front, measure the vertical distance from the head of a first-floor window to the underside of the cornice, and divide by the window's own height. A real Cape reads under 0.25; the raised-eave revival reads 0.5 to 0.9. Second measure: wall height (grade to eave) over total elevation height (grade to ridge). A Cape is about 1:3; the fault is 1:2 or greater. Third and fastest, from any distance: if there is a continuous band of blank siding between the upstairs of the windows and the cornice, the eave has been raised.

exceptions.why: A story-and-a-half Greek Revival house DOES carry a 2-4 ft knee wall above the first-floor window heads - and it makes that knee wall a deep frieze board with horizontal attic windows set into it. The frieze-band window is the honest resolution of exactly this problem, and no other American style does it.
exceptions.bounds: The knee wall must be expressed as a frieze band 10-20 in deep with the attic windows inside it, not as blank siding. The moment the band is siding rather than frieze, the licence ends.

bounds_test.note: The knee wall must be expressed as a frieze band with the attic windows set INSIDE it. The moment the band is siding rather than frieze, the licence ends.

exceptions.why: Same device, at higher finish: the frieze-band attic window under a deep entablature is a defining tell of the style.
exceptions.bounds: As above; and the entablature must be one quarter to one fifth of the column or pilaster height.

bounds_test.note: The frieze-band window only works under a real entablature at one quarter to one fifth of the column height.

exceptions.why: The story-and-a-half farmhouse legitimately runs a knee wall to give upstairs headroom, and does not claim to be a Cape.
exceptions.bounds: It must not then take on the Cape's other signatures - the central chimney, the 32-38 ft five-bay front, the eaveless rake - because those together make a claim the wall height contradicts.

bounds_test.note: Central chimney, 32-38 ft five-bay front, eaveless rake. Take on more than one of these and the wall height starts contradicting a claim the building is making.

exceptions.why: A full second storey inside the roof is the type's whole purpose, achieved by the gambrel's 20:12-24:12 lower slope rather than by raising the eave.
exceptions.bounds: By the gambrel, not by the plate: wall height to eave 9-12 ft is one storey plus knee wall, and above that the gambrel must do the work.

bounds_test.note: One storey plus knee wall. Above that the gambrel's 20:12-24:12 lower slope must be doing the work, not the plate.

inverted_by.statement: The eave DOWN is the fault. Dropping the cornice to the first-floor window heads on a two-storey formal house turns the second storey into a half storey and destroys the graduation the composition depends on.
As above - the second storey is meant to be full height and to overhang.

confused_with.difference: That fault is about the relation of two full storeys to each other. This one is about a type whose defining measurement is the height of a single plate.

deprecated_inheritance.statement: The Cape's authentic interior dimensions - a 6 ft 10 in to 7 ft 6 in ground-floor ceiling and a loft 6 ft 0 in to 7 ft 0 in at the ridge - are correct for the type and were built that way for two centuries.
deprecated_inheritance.why_not_to_inherit: The loft dimension is below the IRC R305.1 minimum of 7 ft 0 in for habitable space, so it cannot be reproduced literally in a bedroom today; and the pressure to make it legal is exactly what raises the eave and destroys the type.
deprecated_inheritance.modern_substitute: Take the headroom from pitch and depth rather than from plate height: 11:12 or 12:12 over a 28-30 ft depth gives a compliant upper floor at a Cape eave. Where that is not enough, put the difference in a rear shed dormer, which the type admits as a later addition, and leave the street elevation alone.

sources: IRC R305.1 and R305.1.1 (ceiling heights, sloped ceilings)
HABS documentation of Cape Cod and Barnstable County houses
Ernest Allen Connally, 'The Cape Cod House: An Introductory Study', JSAH 19 (1960)
